topics: 🧵 'Or a Garment' — the extra word that brings small swatches into tzaraat and sheretz impurity
🐫 Camel's Hair and Silk — the school of Rabbi Yishmael's list of fabrics beyond wool and linen
🚫 Kilayim and Tzitzit — does 'or a garment' teach forbidden mixtures or the fringes obligation instead?
👁️ The Blind Man's Cloak — why tzitzit applies to a garment a blind person cannot see, but not to nightwear
🌳 New Mishna: Flax Alone — the one tree-product fit for the Shabbat lamp and for tent-impurity over a corpse
📜 Why Flax Counts as 'Tree' — Rahab's flax stalks on the roof in the Book of Joshua

overview.title: 📖 Overview: From 'Or a Garment' to Flax Alone
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 27a–27b
overview.hebrewSource: כׇּל הַיּוֹצֵא מִן הָעֵץ אֵין מַדְלִיקִין בּוֹ, אֶלָּא פִּשְׁתָּן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara continues tracing the sources for which fabrics can contract ritual impurity, now focusing on the extra word 'or' in 'or a garment' (Leviticus 11:32) and what it comes to include — small wool/linen swatches, or entirely different fabrics like camel's hair and silk. Abaye, Rava, Rav Pappa, and Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak each propose a different use for the derivation, including whether it teaches the laws of kilayim (forbidden mixtures) or tzitzit, and why a blind person's garment is obligated in tzitzit while a night garment is not. The daf then reaches a new mishna: of everything that grows from a tree, only flax may be used for the Shabbat lamp, and only flax can contract tent-impurity over a corpse — a rule the Gemara supports from the story of Rahab hiding Joshua's spies under flax stalks on her roof.

slides.title: 🧵 What Does 'Or a Garment' Add?
slides.subtitle: Abaye and Rava read the extra word differently

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: 'Garment' alone teaches only a whole garment. From where do we include a three-by-three swatch of other fabrics? The verse says: אוֹ בֶגֶד, 'or a garment' (Leviticus 11:32).

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: But I hold other fabrics never become impure at all! I use 'or a garment' instead to include a wool/linen swatch of three by three fingerbreadths for sheretz impurity.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: No extra verse is even needed for sheretz — the Torah already revealed this rule for tzaraat, and the same applies to sheretz.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: That comparison fails: tzaraat is more stringent, since even warp and woof threads alone can become impure from it.

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: The two amoraim keep sparring over exactly what work the word 'or' is doing — and for whom.

slides.title: 🐫 What Fabrics Does 'Or a Garment' Include?
slides.subtitle: Four amoraim, four different answers
rows: Includes camel's hair, rabbit's wool, goat hair, silk (shirayin, kalakh, serikin) as impurity-susceptible fabrics
Distinguishes three-by-three fingerbreadths (not impure) from three-by-three handbreadths (impure) in other garments
Suggested it teaches that kilayim (wool-linen mixture) applies even to merely placing a garment on oneself — rejected as mistaken
It teaches that the mitzva of tzitzit applies only to wool and linen garments

callout.label: Rav Pappa's view rejected:
callout.text: An a fortiori argument shows that if wearing a mixture (full-body benefit) is limited to wool and linen, merely placing it on oneself must be even more limited — so his statement was called 'a mistake.'

slides.title: 👁️ Whose Garment Needs Tzitzit?
slides.subtitle: Deriving the blind person's obligation, and nightwear's exemption

nodes.content: ❓ Numbers 15:39 — tzitzit is 'that you may look upon it.' Does this exclude a night garment, or a blind person's garment?
📜 Deuteronomy 22:12 says tzitzit go on 'your covering, with which you cover yourself' — this includes a blind person's garment, since he too covers himself

columns.label: Included
columns.content: A blind person's garment — it is visible to others, even if not to him

columns.label: Excluded
columns.content: A night garment — not visible to anyone, so 'that you may look upon it' excludes it

callout.label: Why not other fabrics?
callout.text: Since the verse is already discussing a wool/linen garment, its amplification naturally extends only to another wool/linen garment — not to unrelated fabrics.

slides.title: 🌳 New Mishna: Only Flax Comes From a Tree
slides.subtitle: Two rules share one exception
slides.hebrewSource: כׇּל הַיּוֹצֵא מִן הָעֵץ אֵין מַדְלִיקִין בּוֹ, אֶלָּא פִּשְׁתָּן. וְכׇל הַיּוֹצֵא מִן הָעֵץ אֵינוֹ מִטַּמֵּא טוּמְאַת אֹהָלִים, אֶלָּא פִּשְׁתָּן
slides.label: The mishna:
slides.text: Of everything that grows from a tree, only flax may be used to light the Shabbat lamp — other tree products burn poorly. And of everything that grows from a tree, only flax can become impure through tent-impurity over a corpse: if a house or tent made of flax covers a corpse, the tent itself becomes impure, unlike tents made of other tree-derived materials.

steps.content: 1️⃣ Question: Flax does not look like a tree at all — where do we learn it counts as one?
2️⃣ Mar Zutra's proof: Joshua 2:6 — Rahab hid the spies 'under the פִּשְׁתֵּי הָעֵץ', the trees of flax, on her roof
3️⃣ Second question: why does only flax (among tree products) contract tent-impurity over a corpse?
4️⃣ Rabbi Elazar's answer: a verbal analogy (gezera shava) links the word 'tent' used regarding impurity to the word 'tent' used elsewhere about flax

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: Both special rules for flax — as lamp fuel and as tent-impurity conductor — rest on flax's unique scriptural classification as a 'tree' product.

summary.principle: The word 'or' in 'or a garment' generates several halakhot — which small fabric swatches become impure, which materials are obligated in tzitzit — while a new mishna singles out flax as the one tree product usable for the Shabbat lamp and susceptible to tent-impurity, both traced to its scriptural label as a 'tree.'

flowSteps.content: 🧵 'Or a garment' (Lev. 11:32) — Abaye and Rava dispute what it includes
🐫 Possible readings: camel's hair/silk fabrics, three-by-three handbreadth swatches, kilayim, or tzitzit

columns.content: 👁️ Tzitzit applies to a blind person's visible-to-others garment, not to night garments
🌳 New mishna: only flax may light the lamp or carry tent-impurity among tree products

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Flax's unique status as scriptural 'tree' (Joshua 2:6) underlies both of its special Shabbat-lamp and impurity rules

quiz.q: According to the baraita, what does the extra word 'or' in 'or a garment' (Leviticus 11:32) come to include?
o: Only garments made of silk
A three-by-three handbreadth swatch of fabrics other than wool or linen becoming ritually impure
The prohibition of kilayim
The obligation of tzitzit on all garments
quiz.e: The baraita states that 'garment' alone teaches only a whole garment; 'or a garment' comes to include a three-by-three swatch of other fabrics.

quiz.q: Why does Abaye reject using leprosy's impurity rules to derive sheretz (creeping animal) impurity rules for small swatches?
o: Because sheretz impurity does not exist
Because leprosy is more stringent — even warp and woof threads alone can become impure from it, unlike sheretz
Because swatches can never become impure
Because the Torah never discusses sheretz impurity
quiz.e: Abaye argues the comparison fails because tzaraat (leprosy) impurity is more stringent than sheretz impurity, since even loose warp/woof threads contract tzaraat impurity.

quiz.q: Why was Rav Pappa's proposed derivation about kilayim (wool-linen mixtures) rejected?
o: Because kilayim is never forbidden

Because an a fortiori inference shows that if full wearing benefit is restricted to wool and linen, merely placing the garment on oneself should be even more restricted, making the derivation unnecessary and wrong
Because Deuteronomy never mentions kilayim
Because Rav Pappa retracted it himself
quiz.e: The Gemara rejects Rav Pappa's statement with an a fortiori argument, concluding it must be a mistaken attribution.

quiz.q: Why is a blind person's garment obligated in tzitzit, while a night garment is exempt?
o: Because blind people are exempt from all mitzvot
Because a blind person's garment is visible to other people even though he cannot see it himself, while a night garment is not visible to anyone
Because night garments are made of different material
Because tzitzit only apply to daytime wear by law
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that 'that you may look upon it' excludes only what is invisible to everyone (a night garment); a blind person's garment remains visible to others, so it is included.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what is unique about flax among substances that grow from a tree?
o: It is the only one forbidden for any use
It is the only tree product that may be used to light the Shabbat lamp and the only one that can transmit tent-impurity over a corpse
It is the only tree product used for tzitzit
It cannot be woven into fabric
quiz.e: The mishna states that of everything from a tree, only flax may fuel the Shabbat lamp, and only flax (among tree products) can become impure via tent-impurity over a corpse.
